To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we propose a method to compose photorealistic scenes by learning per-object neural scattering functions that model light transport between objects and lights, which enables us to render multi-object scenes in novel lighting and object configurations.

1) we present a method for rendering multi-object scenes by composing OSFs, 2) we show how OSFs can be used for novel view synthesis, 3) OSFs can model the light transport of objects, 4) OSFs can be trained in a self-supervised fashion using a volumetric path tracer, and 5) our method is able to generalize to novel scenes, even when objects and lights are in new configurations
We present an implicit neural representation that models the volumetric scattering properties of objects.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing a neural representation of the physical world that is able to render scenes with multiple objects in a photorealistic manner, and that can generalize to unseen object configurations.

the following problem: given an object-centric neural scene representation, can we render photorealistic images? We propose an approach based on a neural representation of light transport that enables us to render scenes with moving objects, new lighting, and new camera viewpoints.

the following question: Can we use a neural representation that models the scattering properties of objects to render photorealistic scenes of multiple objects under novel illumination and view conditions?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our work enables the creation of photorealistic, realistic, and physically accurate scenes, even when objects or lighting conditions change.
we present a method that enables the rendering of realistic scenes of multiple objects from captured images, even when the objects or lighting change.
the proposed method enables the rendering of photorealistic, multi-object, dynamic scenes from images alone, without requiring any underlying 3D models.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we propose to learn a neural scattering field that can model per-object light transport.
we propose to learn a representation of light transport that can be used to render a scene from novel viewpoints and lighting.
we present a method that can render a scene with objects from images, without any 3D model or scene information.
The main takeaway from our work is that

neural representations are a promising direction for learning physically-based models of light transport, and can be applied to many different tasks, including novel view synthesis, relighting, and inverse rendering.
object-centric representations are a promising direction to enable generalizable neural scene representations that can be used in a variety of applications, from image synthesis to 3D reconstruction.
we can learn object-centric neural representations that can be composed into scenes, enabling the generation of novel photorealistic scenes without retraining.
